{{Short description|Non-diagonalizable matrix; one lacking a basis of eigenvectors}}
{{Use American English|date = April 2019}}
In [[linear algebra]], a '''defective matrix''' is a [[square matrix]] that does not have a complete [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]] of [[eigenvector]]s, and is therefore not [[diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizable]]. In particular, an <math>n \times n</math> [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] is defective [[if and only if]] it does not have <math>n</math> [[linearly independent]] eigenvectors.<ref name="golub">{{harvtxt|Golub|Van Loan|1996|p=316}}</ref> A complete basis is formed by augmenting the eigenvectors with [[generalized eigenvector]]s, which are necessary for solving defective systems of [[ordinary differential equation]]s and other problems.

An <math>n \times n</math> defective matrix always has fewer than <math>n</math> distinct [[eigenvalue]]s, since distinct eigenvalues always have linearly independent eigenvectors. In particular, a defective matrix has one or more eigenvalues <math>\lambda</math> with [[algebraic multiplicity]] <math>m > 1</math> (that is, they are multiple [[root of a polynomial|roots]] of the [[characteristic polynomial]]), but fewer than <math>m</math> linearly independent eigenvectors associated with <math>\lambda</math>. If the algebraic multiplicity of <math>\lambda</math> exceeds its [[geometric multiplicity]] (that is, the number of linearly independent eigenvectors associated with <math>\lambda</math>), then <math>\lambda</math> is said to be a '''defective eigenvalue'''.<ref name="golub"/> However, every eigenvalue with algebraic multiplicity <math>m</math> always has <math>m</math> linearly independent generalized eigenvectors.

A [[real number|real]] [[symmetric matrix]] and more generally a [[Hermitian matrix]], and a [[unitary matrix]], is never defective; more generally, a [[normal matrix]] (which includes Hermitian and unitary matrices as special cases) is never defective.

==Jordan block==

Any nontrivial [[Jordan matrix|Jordan block]] of size <math>2 \times 2</math> or larger (that is, not completely diagonal) is defective. (A diagonal matrix is a special case of the Jordan normal form with all trivial Jordan blocks of size <math>1 \times 1</math> and is not defective.) For example, the <math>n \times n</math> Jordan block
:<math>J = \begin{bmatrix}
\lambda & 1            & \;     & \;  \\
\;        & \lambda    & \ddots & \;  \\
\;        & \;           & \ddots & 1   \\
\;        & \;           & \;     & \lambda       
\end{bmatrix},</math>
has an [[eigenvalue]], <math>\lambda</math> with algebraic multiplicity <math>n</math> (or greater if there are other Jordan blocks with the same eigenvalue), but only one distinct eigenvector <math> J v_1 = \lambda v_1 </math>, where <math>v_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.</math> The other canonical basis vectors <math>v_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, ~ \ldots, ~ v_n = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}</math> form a chain of generalized eigenvectors such that <math>J v_k = \lambda v_k + v_{k-1}</math> for <math>k=2,\ldots,n </math>.

Any defective matrix has a nontrivial [[Jordan normal form]], which is as close as one can come to [[matrix diagonalization|diagonalization]] of such a matrix.

==Example==

A simple example of a defective matrix is
:<math>\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix},</math>
which has a double [[eigenvalue]] of 3 but only one distinct eigenvector
:<math>\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}</math>
(and constant multiples thereof).
